source: library/titles.html (certified 2026-07-17) — Son of Man / Daniel 7 / the trial / Kyrios, plus the essay's own cumulative-pattern bound
voiceover: Jesus' favourite name for himself was Son of Man. It appears about eighty times in the Gospels, almost always on his own lips. And it sounds humble — a human being. That is how God addresses the prophet Ezekiel, and that ordinary sense is real. But the background is Daniel chapter seven. There the prophet sees one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approaches the Ancient of Days, and receives a kingdom that never ends. And coming with the clouds is imagery the Hebrew Bible uses of God's own appearing. So at his trial, Jesus fuses Daniel seven with Psalm one hundred and ten, and claims to be the heavenly figure enthroned beside God. Then there is Lord. Kyrios. When the Greek Old Testament was read aloud in the synagogues, the divine name was regularly spoken as Kyrios. And Paul writes: if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved — for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. He is quoting a line about calling on YHWH. No single title settles it, and we should say so. Messiah and Son of David are royal, and human. But read together, they place Jesus inside what Israel reserved for her God alone — and that is a remarkable place for the evidence to begin.
